common_name: Mel's Blue Stokes' Aster (Compact Chance-Seedling Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in lean, sharply drained, slightly acidic soil; Mel's Blue tolerates a few hours of afternoon shade better than most Stokesia selections, an advantage in hot-summer gardens.

directions: Mel's Blue arose as a spontaneous mutation discovered on a Dutch nursery block in 2007 and has since become one of the most widely sold Stokes' aster selections for its unusually compact, tidy clump. Cornflower-like violet-blue flowers with a paler, almost white center open smaller and more numerous than the larger blooms of 'Blue Danube' already in this dataset, and the tighter basal rosette holds up without staking. Plant divisions in spring in lean, sharply drained soil; established clumps tolerate a few hours of afternoon shade better than most other Stokesia selections. Deadhead spent flower heads to extend the bloom season into early fall.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in lean, sharply drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; crowns are prone to rot in soggy winter ground, so drainage matters more than fertility.

directions: Alba is one of the oldest white-flowered forms of Stokes' aster in cultivation, predating patented introductions such as 'Silver Moon' and 'Divinity' already in this dataset, and its fringed, cornflower-like blooms open in a slightly looser, more informal shape than those newer selections. The pure white petals surround a small pale-yellow center and are held on stiff stems above a low evergreen rosette of lance-shaped leaves. Give it sharply drained, lean soil, since like the rest of the species it is prone to crown rot in soggy winter ground, and site it where a bit of midday shade tempers summer heat without slowing bloom. Divide congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Zestful Pacific Bleeding Heart (Deep Rose Fernleaf Selection)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring in cool, humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in shade; foliage scorches and the plant goes dormant early if the site dries out or gets too much summer sun.

directions: Zestful is a selection of the Pacific Northwest native Dicentra formosa chosen for flowers in a noticeably deeper, more saturated rose-pink than the soft pink of the wild species and of related selections such as 'Bacchanal' already in this dataset. Its finely dissected, blue-green fernlike foliage spreads by shallow, brittle rhizomes to form an expanding woodland groundcover under conifers and deciduous canopy. Plant divisions in cool, humus-rich, consistently moist soil in shade, since the foliage scorches and the plant goes dormant early if the site dries out or gets too much summer sun. It self-sows lightly in favorable woodland conditions but is not aggressive.

planting.note: Plant divisions in gritty, fast-draining, humus-poor soil that mimics native serpentine substrate, in full to partial shade with reliable moisture during active growth.

directions: This regionally rare subspecies is restricted in the wild to serpentine-derived soils of the Klamath-Siskiyou Mountains along the Oregon-California border, where it is easily told apart from typical Dicentra formosa by its cream to pale-yellow flowers rather than the pink or purple tones of the species and its cultivars elsewhere in this dataset. Its finely cut leaves carry a distinct blue-gray, glaucous bloom on both surfaces, giving the whole plant a cooler, silvery cast. Grow it in gritty, fast-draining, humus-poor soil that mimics its native serpentine substrate, in full to partial shade with reliable moisture during active growth. It is slower to spread by rhizome than the coastal Pacific bleeding heart and best suited to specialty native-plant and rock-garden collections.
sources: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Species Profile

common_name: Snowdrift Fringed Bleeding Heart (Everblooming White Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade in spring; mulch to keep roots cool through summer heat and extend repeat bloom.

directions: Snowdrift pairs the heat tolerance and long, repeat-blooming habit of the Appalachian native Dicentra eximia with pure white, dangling, heart-shaped flowers, distinguishing it from the rose-pink species already in this dataset and from the Pacific-heritage whites 'Aurora' and 'Ivory Hearts' by its finer, more heat-resistant blue-gray foliage. Flowering begins in spring and continues intermittently into fall wherever soil moisture is maintained, since unlike the Asian common bleeding heart it does not go summer-dormant. Plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade, and mulch to keep roots cool through summer heat. It self-sows modestly, gradually forming a naturalized colony without becoming aggressive.

common_name: Louisiana Purple Woodland Phlox (Fragrant Maroon-Eyed Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in early spring or fall in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade with good air movement to limit powdery mildew.

directions: Louisiana Purple originated as a wild selection of woodland phlox found near the Gulf Coast and is valued for opening its fragrant violet-purple flowers, each marked with a contrasting dark maroon eye, earlier than typical wild blue phlox and the other named selections already in this dataset. Its compact, low-spreading evergreen foliage stays tidy through the growing season and knits together into a dense mat under deciduous trees. Plant divisions in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade, and provide good air movement to limit powdery mildew on the foliage after bloom. Shear lightly once flowering ends to keep the mat compact and encourage fresh growth.

common_name: Plum Perfect Woodland Phlox (Vanilla-Scented Magenta Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with strong air circulation, since this selection is more prone to powdery mildew than sturdier woodland phlox cultivars.

directions: Plum Perfect bears lavender-plum flowers deepening to a dark red-purple eye zone and carries a faint vanilla fragrance, a richer, more saturated color combination than the blue-violet tones of most woodland phlox selections already in this dataset. Growth is low and loosely spreading rather than densely mounding, giving it a more open, informal texture at the front of a shaded border. Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with strong air circulation, since trial evaluations have found it more prone to powdery mildew and generally less vigorous than top-performing selections such as 'Chattahoochee'. Site it where afternoon shade and good airflow can offset that susceptibility.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center Trial Garden Report

planting.note: Set out divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade with good air circulation, watering well until the mat is established.

directions: Iridescens produces lavender-pink flowers with a faintly luminous sheen across the petals, giving plantings a subtly different color note from the deep violet-blue of 'Sherwood Purple' already in this dataset. Like other creeping phlox selections it spreads by rooting stolons into a dense, semi-evergreen mat useful for shaded slopes and woodland paths. Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade, and prioritize good air circulation, since trial evaluations have found this selection more susceptible to summer powdery mildew than sturdier cultivars as its mat fills in. Shear lightly after bloom and divide crowded patches every few years to maintain a healthy, open habit.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center Trial Garden Report
